zajjaj:1-1.t:
Sūrat al-Insān
Meccan
﷽
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿هَلْ أتى عَلى الإنْسانِ حِينٌ مِنَ الدَّهْرِ لَمْ يَكُنْ شَيْئًا مَذْكُورًا﴾: the meaning is: "Has there not come upon man a period of time when he was already something" — except that he was dust and clay until the spirit was breathed into him? — "so before the spirit was breathed into him he was not a thing mentioned." It is also possible that all people are meant by it, the meaning being that they were drops of sperm, then clinging clots, then lumps of flesh, until they became a thing mentioned. The meaning of ﴿هَلْ أتى﴾ is "there has indeed come upon man", that is: "Has there not come upon man a period of time…?"

zajjaj:2-2.t: His saying: ﴿إنّا خَلَقْنا الإنْسانَ مِن نُطْفَةٍ أمْشاجٍ نَبْتَلِيهِ﴾: «أمْشاجٍ» means mixtures — sperm and blood — then he is moved from one state to another. The singular of الأمْشاج is «مَشَجٌ». The meaning of «نَبْتَلِيهِ» is: We test him. What points to this is: ﴿فَجَعَلْناهُ سَمِيعًا بَصِيرًا﴾, that is: "We made him so in order to test him."

zajjaj:3-3.t: His saying: ﴿إنّا هَدَيْناهُ السَّبِيلَ إمّا شاكِرًا وإمّا كَفُورًا﴾: its meaning is: We guided him to the way, whether to wretchedness or to felicity.

zajjaj:4-4.t: His saying: ﴿سَلاسِلَ وأغْلالا وسَعِيرًا﴾: the best usage in Arabic is that «سَلاسِلَ» not be declined as a triptote (i.e. that it be treated as a diptote), but since it was made the end of a verse it was given nunation, so that the ends of the verses would be on one pattern.

zajjaj:5-5.t:
His saying: ﴿إنَّ الأبْرارَ يَشْرَبُونَ مِن كَأْسٍ﴾: «اَلْأبْرارُ», its singular is «بَرٌّ». ﴿يَشْرَبُونَ مِن كَأْسٍ كانَ مِزاجُها كافُورًا﴾: linguistically it may be that the taste of fragrance and of camphor is in it, and it is possible that it is mixed with camphor without any harm in that, because the people of the Garden are touched by no harm and no fatigue in what they eat and drink. «اَلْكَأْسُ» in the language is the vessel when there is drink in it; when there is no drink in it, it is not called a كَأْس. The poet said:
؎صَدَدْتِ الكَأْسَ عَنّا أُمَّ عَمْرٍو ∗∗∗ وكانَ الكَأْسُ مَجْراها اليَمِينا
(You turned the cup away from us, O Umm ʿAmr, though the cup's course was to pass to the right.)

zajjaj:6-6.t: His saying: ﴿عَيْنًا يَشْرَبُ بِها عِبادُ اللَّهِ﴾: «عَيْنًا» may be part of the description of the cup, but the better view is that the meaning is "from a spring". His saying: ﴿يُفَجِّرُونَها تَفْجِيرًا﴾ means: "that spring flows for them as they wish."

zajjaj:7-7.t: His saying: ﴿كانَ شَرُّهُ مُسْتَطِيرًا﴾: its meaning is: it reaches the utmost extent.

zajjaj:8-8.t: His saying: ﴿وَيُطْعِمُونَ الطَّعامَ عَلى حُبِّهِ مِسْكِينًا﴾: this hāʾ (pronoun) refers back to the food. The meaning is: they give food to the poor man when their own need for it is at its most severe; and Allah described them as preferring others over themselves. ﴿وَيَتِيمًا وأسِيرًا﴾: «اَلْأسِيرُ» (the captive) — it was said that at that time he was one of the unbelievers. And whoever feeds a captive was praised, though he is an unbeliever — so how much more the Muslim captives! This indicates that in feeding those held in prisons there is abundant reward, and the people of the prisons are captives.

zajjaj:9-9.t: His saying: ﴿إنَّما نُطْعِمُكم لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ لا نُرِيدُ مِنكم جَزاءً ولا شُكُورًا﴾: the meaning is "saying: We feed you only for the countenance of Allah", that is: seeking the reward of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is possible that they fed without uttering these words, but this was their intention in feeding, so what was in their hearts was expressed in words. Likewise: ﴿إنّا نَخافُ مِن رَبِّنا يَوْمًا عَبُوسًا قَمْطَرِيرًا﴾ [al-Insān: 10]. «اَلْعُبُوسُ» is that which makes faces frown; this is like His saying: ﴿وَوُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ باسِرَةٌ﴾ [al-Qiyāma: 24]. As for «قَمْطَرِيرًا», one says «يَوْمٌ قَمْطَرِيرٌ» and «يَوْمٌ قُماطِرٌ» when it is severe and harsh. It has come in the exegesis that «قَمْطَرِيرًا» means: it frowns so that what is between the eyes is drawn together; and this is acceptable in the language: one says «اِقْمَطَرَّتِ النّاقَةُ» when the she-camel raises her tail, draws her flanks together and thrusts out her nose.

zajjaj:13-13.t: His saying: ﴿مُتَّكِئِينَ فِيها عَلى الأرائِكِ﴾: its singular is «أرِيكَةٌ». It has come in the exegesis that they are of the curtained canopies containing bedding and couches; and in the language every thing reclined upon is an «أرِيكَةٌ». ﴿مُتَّكِئِينَ﴾ is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial); the meaning is: "and He rewarded them with a Garden while they are reclining in it." Likewise: ﴿وَدانِيَةً عَلَيْهِمْ ظِلالُها وذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها تَذْلِيلا﴾ [al-Insān: 14]. It is also possible that «دانِيَةً» is a naʿt (adjective) of the Garden; the meaning is: "and He rewarded them with a Garden whose shades are close over them."

zajjaj:14-14.t: ﴿وَذُلِّلَتْ قُطُوفُها تَذْلِيلا﴾: this is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿قُطُوفُها دانِيَةٌ﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa: 23]. It was said: whenever they want to pick something of it, it is made easy for them and comes near to them, whether they are sitting, lying down or standing.

zajjaj:15-15.t: ﴿وَيُطافُ عَلَيْهِمْ بِآنِيَةٍ مِن فِضَّةٍ وأكْوابٍ كانَتْ قَوارِيرا﴾ ﴿قَوارِيرا﴾ [al-Insān: 16]: it was read without nunation (as a diptote), and this is the preferred choice of the Basran grammarians, because every plural that has two letters after its alif is diptote; we have explained this earlier in the book. Whoever read «قَوارِيرًا», giving nunation to the first, did so because it is the end of a verse, and left the second without nunation because it is not the end of a verse. Whoever gave nunation to the second made the word follow the word, because the Arabs sometimes alter the case-ending of a thing so that the word follows the word, saying «هَذا جُحْرُ ضَبٍّ خَرِبٍ» ("this is a ruined lizard's hole"), whereas خَرِب is really the adjective of the hole — so how much more with what is left undeclined! And everything that is left undeclined may be given nunation in poetry.

zajjaj:16-16.t: The meaning of ﴿قَوارِيرا مِن فِضَّةٍ قَدَّرُوها تَقْدِيرًا﴾: the origin of the glass vessels (qawārīr) of this world is from sand, so Allah made known that the excellence of those vessels is that their origin is of silver, what is inside them being seen from their outside. The meaning of ﴿قَدَّرُوها تَقْدِيرًا﴾ is: they were made such that the vessel is according to the measure of what they need and want. It was also read «قُدِّرُوها تَقْدِيرًا», that is: they were made for them according to the measure of their wish.

zajjaj:17-17.t:
﴿وَيُسْقَوْنَ فِيها كَأْسًا كانَ مِزاجُها زَنْجَبِيلا﴾, that is: it combines the taste of ginger. The Arabs describe ginger, and it is very much relished by them. The poet said:
؎كَأنَّ القَرَنْفُلَ والزَّنْجَبِيلَ ∗∗∗ باتا بِفِيها وأرْيًا مَشُورا
(As though cloves and ginger had spent the night in her mouth, and gathered honey.)
So it may be that the taste of ginger is in it, and it may be that ginger is its mixture without any ill effect from it, as we said regarding camphor.

zajjaj:18-18.t: His saying: ﴿عَيْنًا فِيها تُسَمّى سَلْسَبِيلا﴾: the meaning is "they are given to drink from a spring". «سَلْسَبِيلُ» is the name of the spring, except that it was given nunation because it is the end of a verse. «سَلْسَبِيلُ» in the language is a description of whatever is extremely smooth-flowing, so it is as though the spring — and Allah knows best — was named by its description.

zajjaj:19-19.t:
﴿وَيَطُوفُ عَلَيْهِمْ وِلْدانٌ مُخَلَّدُونَ﴾, that is: youthful servants, made everlasting, serve them. The interpretation of ﴿مُخَلَّدُونَ﴾ is: none of them ever passes beyond the age of youthful service; he remains a youthful servant. The Arabs say of a man who does not grow grey: «هُوَ مُخَلَّدٌ». It is also said that «مُخَلَّدُونَ» means: adorned, wearing ornaments; and a set of ornaments is called «اَلْخَلَدَةُ».
His saying: ﴿حَسِبْتَهم لُؤْلُؤًا مَنثُورًا﴾, that is: in the beauty and purity of their colours they are like scattered pearls.

zajjaj:20-20.t: His saying: ﴿وَإذا رَأيْتَ ثَمَّ رَأيْتَ نَعِيمًا ومُلْكًا كَبِيرًا﴾: it has come in the exegesis that «مُلْكًا كَبِيرًا» means that the angels greet them with peace; and it has also come: the angels ask their permission to enter. «ثَمَّ» (there) refers to the Garden. What governs (al-ʿāmil) «ثَمَّ» is the meaning of «رَأيْتَ»; the meaning is: "and when you see with your sight there". It was also said that the meaning is: "and when you see what is there, you see bliss", but this is a mistake, because on this interpretation «ما» would be a relative noun whose ṣila (relative clause) is «ثَمَّ», and it is not permissible to drop the relative noun and leave its ṣila. Rather, «رَأيْتَ» extends in meaning to «ثَمَّ».

zajjaj:21-21.t:
His saying: «عالِيهِمْ ثِيابُ سُنْدُسٍ», with the yāʾ unvowelled; it was also read ﴿عالِيَهُمْ﴾ with the yāʾ vowelled with fatḥa, and it was read «عَلَيْهِمْ» without alif, ﴿ثِيابُ سُنْدُسٍ﴾. These three agree with the written codex (al-muṣḥaf), and all of them are good in Arabic. It was also read in two ways other than these three: it was read «عالِيَتُهم ثِيابُ سُنْدُسٍ» in the nominative and the feminine, and «عالِيَتَهُمْ» in the accusative. These two ways are good in Arabic, except that they differ from the codex, and I do not consider reading with them acceptable; the readers of the great cities do not read with them.
As for the explanation of the unvowelled «عالِيهِمْ», with the yāʾ unvowelled: it is nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), and its khabar (predicate) is ﴿ثِيابُ سُنْدُسٍ خُضْرٌ﴾. As for whoever put it in the accusative and said ﴿عالِيَهُمْ﴾ with fatḥa on the yāʾ, one of the grammarians said that he makes it accusative as an adverb of place (ẓarf), as you say «فَوْقَهم ثِيابٌ» ("above them are garments"). But we do not know this among the adverbs; and if it were an adverb, it would not be permissible to make the yāʾ unvowelled. Rather, its accusative is as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from one of two things. One of them is from the hāʾ and mīm (-hum); the meaning is: "youthful servants made everlasting go round among the righteous, garments of fine silk being upon the righteous" — because He has described their states in the Garden, so the meaning is: "these go round among them in this state." It may also be a ḥāl from the youthful servants; the meaning is: "when you see them you would think them scattered pearls, in the state of the garments being over them." So the accusative on this account is clear.
As for «عَلَيْهِمْ ثِيابُ سُنْدُسٍ», it is nominative, as when you say «عَلَيْكَ مالٌ» ("you owe money"): you put it in the nominative as a mubtadaʾ, and the meaning is: "and garments of fine silk are upon them." The explanation of the accusative and nominative of «عالِيَتَهُمْ» is like the explanation of «عالِيَهُمْ».
«اَلسُّنْدُسُ» is silk. It was read «خُضْرٌ» and «خُضْرٍ». Whoever read «خُضْرٌ» — and this is better — makes it a naʿt (adjective) of the garments, since the word الثِّياب is a plural word and «خُضْرٌ» is a plural word. Whoever read «خُضْرٍ» makes it an adjective of السُّنْدُس, and «اَلسُّنْدُسُ» in meaning refers back to the garments.
It was read «وَإسْتَبْرَقٌ» — which is thick, heavy, coarse brocade — and it was read in the nominative and in the genitive. Whoever put it in the nominative conjoined it to «ثِيابُ»; the meaning is: "upon them is brocade (إسْتَبْرَقٌ)." Whoever put it in the genitive conjoined it to السُّنْدُس, and the meaning is: "upon them are garments of these two kinds, garments of fine silk and brocade."
It was also read «وَإسْتَبْرَقَ» in two ways other than these two, both of them very weak in Arabic. It was read «وَإسْتَبْرَقَ وحُلُّوا», with إسْتَبْرَقَ in the accusative form while it is in a genitive position, not given nunation; Ibn Muḥayṣin read it so. They claimed that he did not give it nunation because «وَإسْتَبْرَقَ» is a foreign noun, its origin in Persian being «اِسْتَبْرَهُ», so when it was transferred into Arabic it was not declined. This is a mistake, because it is indefinite — do you not see that the alif and lām enter it? You say: «اَلسُّنْدُسُ والإسْتَبْرَقُ». The second way is «واسْتَبْرَقَ وحُلُّوا», dropping the alif: he made the alif a connective alif (alif al-waṣl) and made it something named with the verb derived from al-barīq (gleaming). This is an error, because الإسْتَبْرَق is known — it is well known that it is a noun transferred from Persian into Arabic, just as الدِّيباج (brocade) was named, which is likewise transferred from Persian.
His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَسَقاهم رَبُّهم شَرابًا طَهُورًا﴾: it has come in the exegesis that when they drink it their bellies become lean and their skins exude sweat like the scent of musk. It was also said that it is pure, not filth like the wine of this world.

zajjaj:24-24.t: His saying: ﴿وَلا تُطِعْ مِنهم آثِمًا أوْ كَفُورًا﴾: «أوْ» here is more emphatic than the wāw. For with the wāw, if you say «لا تُطِعْ زَيْدًا وعَمْرًا» ("do not obey Zayd and ʿAmr") and he obeys one of the two, he is not disobedient, because he commanded him not to obey the two together. But when He said ﴿وَلا تُطِعْ مِنهم آثِمًا أوْ كَفُورًا﴾, «أوْ» indicated that each one of them deserves to be disobeyed. Likewise, when you say «لا تُخالِفِ الحَسَنَ أوِ ابْنَ سِيرِينَ» ("do not oppose al-Ḥasan or Ibn Sīrīn") or «اِتَّبِعِ الحَسَنَ أوِ ابْنَ سِيرِينَ» ("follow al-Ḥasan or Ibn Sīrīn"), you have said: "These two deserve to be followed," and each one of them is deserving. We have given the like of this explanation for a word other than this one at the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqara, in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿مَثَلُهم كَمَثَلِ الَّذِي اسْتَوْقَدَ نارًا﴾ [al-Baqara: 17] to the end of the verse, and after that ﴿أوْ كَصَيِّبٍ مِنَ السَّماءِ﴾ [al-Baqara: 19], whose interpretation is the same: for whether you liken them to the one who kindled a fire, or liken them to the rainstorm, or to both together, you are correct.

zajjaj:25-25.t: His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿واذْكُرِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ بُكْرَةً وأصِيلا﴾: «اَلْأصِيلُ» is the late afternoon/evening (al-ʿashiyy). One says «قَدْ أصَلْنا» ("we have entered the aṣīl") when they enter the aṣīl, which is the ʿashiyy.

zajjaj:28-28.t: His saying: ﴿نَحْنُ خَلَقْناهم وشَدَدْنا أسْرَهُمْ﴾: «أسْرَهُمْ» means their make (khalq). It has also come in the exegesis: their joints.

zajjaj:30-30.t: His saying: ﴿وَما تَشاءُونَ إلا أنْ يَشاءَ اللَّهُ إنَّ اللَّهَ كانَ عَلِيمًا حَكِيمًا﴾, that is: you do not will except by the will of Allah.

zajjaj:31-31.t: ﴿والظّالِمِينَ أعَدَّ لَهم عَذابًا ألِيمًا﴾: «الظّالِمِينَ» is in the accusative because what precedes it is accusative. The meaning is: "He admits whom He wills into His mercy, and He punishes the wrongdoers — He has prepared for them a painful punishment," and ﴿أعَدَّ لَهُمْ﴾ is an explanation (tafsīr) of this implied (muḍmar) verb. It was also read «والظّالِمُونَ», but I do not consider reading with it acceptable, for two reasons. One of them is that it differs from the codex. The other is that, even if it is permissible in Arabic — on the basis that «اَلظّالِمِينَ» is put in the nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject) and what comes after «اَلظّالِمِينَ» is the khabar (predicate) of the mubtadaʾ — the preferred choice of the Basran grammarians is the accusative. The grammarians say: «أعْطَيْتُ زَيْدًا وعَمْرًا أعَدَدْتُ لَهُ بُرًّا» ("I gave to Zayd, and ʿAmr — I prepared wheat for him"), and they prefer the accusative in the sense of "and I treated ʿAmr kindly", and «أبَرُّ عَمْرًا أعْدَدْتُ لَهُ بُرًّا». So they choose for the Qur'an nothing but the best of the ways — and this, moreover, in agreement with the codex.
